stem: Which statement best describes a point in geometry?
options: It marks an exact location and has no length, breadth or height.
It is a tiny dot whose fixed length is about one millimetre.
It is a short mark that has length but has no breadth at all.
It is a small circle whose size depends on how sharp the pencil is.
explanation: Correct option: (A). A point only fixes a precise location; it has no length, breadth or height, so a pencil dot is just a model of it. The other options give a point some size (a length, or a size that depends on the pencil), which a geometric point does not have.

stem: Points A and B are marked on a sheet of paper. What is the shortest path from A to B, including A and B, called?
options: The ray from A through B
explanation: Correct option: (C). The shortest path from A to B, including both end points, is the line segment AB (also written BA). A ray has only one starting point and goes on endlessly, a line goes on endlessly in both directions, and an angle needs two rays.

stem: Rihan marks one point on a paper and Sheetal marks two points on another paper. Which statement about the lines they can draw is correct?
options: Rihan can draw exactly one line; Sheetal can draw countless lines.
Rihan can draw many lines; Sheetal can draw exactly one line.
Both of them can draw exactly one line through their points.
Both of them can draw many lines through all their points.
explanation: Correct option: (B). Through a single point, lines can be drawn in countless directions, so Rihan can draw many lines. Two points determine a unique line, so Sheetal can draw exactly one line through both. The other options swap or mix up these two facts.

stem: Five points L, M, P, Q and R are joined in order to make the line segments LM, MP, PQ and QR. Which points lie on exactly two of these line segments?
explanation: Correct option: (B). L lies only on LM and R lies only on QR. M lies on LM and MP, P lies on MP and PQ, and Q lies on PQ and QR, so M, P and Q each lie on two segments. Options with L or R wrongly count the end points, and 'P and Q only' misses M.

stem: A ray starts at point O and passes through point A. Point B also lies on this ray, between O and A. Which other name can be used for this ray?
explanation: Correct option: (A). A ray is named by its starting point first and then any other point on it. The ray starts at O and passes through B, so it can also be named OB. AO and BO would start at A or B, and AB would start at A, so they name different rays.

stem: Ray OA starts at O and passes through A. Can ray OA also be written as ray AO?
options: Yes, because the order of letters never matters for a ray.
No, because AO is a ray that starts at A, so it is different.
Yes, because both of the names use the same two points.
No, because a ray must always be named with only a single letter.
explanation: Correct option: (B). The first letter in a ray's name is its starting point. Ray AO starts at A and goes towards O, while ray OA starts at O, so they are different rays. Using the same two points is not enough, and rays are named with two letters, not one.

stem: Points T, N and B lie on one line in that order, with N between T and B. Point A does not lie on this line. Rays TA, TN, TB and NB are drawn. Which statement is true?
options: Ray NB contains the point T.
Ray TB and ray NB are the same ray.
Ray TN and ray TB are the same ray.
Ray TA contains the point N.
explanation: Correct option: (C). Ray TN starts at T and goes through N, and it continues past B, so it is exactly the same ray as TB. Ray NB starts at N and goes towards B, away from T, so it does not contain T and is not the same as TB (different starting points). N is on line TB, not on ray TA.

options: Two lines that never meet each other
Two rays having a common starting point
One ray and a point that is not on it
Two points joined by the shortest possible path
explanation: Correct option: (B). An angle is formed by two rays with a common starting point, which is its vertex. Lines that never meet form no angle, a ray and a separate point are not two rays, and two points joined by the shortest path form a line segment.

stem: Two angles need the same amount of turn to move one arm onto the other. The arms of the first angle are drawn twice as long as the arms of the second. Which statement is correct?
options: The first angle is twice as large.
The first angle is a little larger.
The two angles are equal in size.
explanation: Correct option: (D). The size of an angle is the amount of rotation about the vertex needed to move one arm onto the other. Both angles need the same turn, so they are equal. Longer arms do not make an angle larger, and shorter arms do not make it larger either.

stem: Two angles are superimposed. Their vertices lie on each other and both arms of one angle lie exactly on the arms of the other. What can be concluded?

They cannot be compared this way.
explanation: Correct option: (B). When the common vertex and both rays of the two angles lie on top of each other, the same amount of rotation is needed in both, so the angles are equal. Neither angle can be larger, and superimposition is exactly the way to compare them.

stem: A transparent circle is placed on the first angle with its centre on the vertex O, and points A and B are marked where the arms cross the edge. On the second angle, the centre is put on its vertex with one arm passing through A, and its other arm crosses the edge beyond B, farther from A. Which conclusion is correct?

stem: An angle-shaped slit is cut in cardboard by tracing one pair of rotating arms. Which pair of rotating arms will pass through the slit, if all arms are shorter than the slit?

A pair with an angle smaller than the slit's angle
Any pair, since all the arms are shorter than it
Only a pair whose angle equals the slit's angle

stem: Rays OA, OX, OY and OB start from O. Turning from OA towards OB, you first meet OX and then OY. Which statement about angle AOB and angle XOY is correct?
options: Angle XOY is greater than angle AOB.
Angle AOB is greater than angle XOY.
They are equal as both have vertex O.
They cannot be compared at all.

stem: A straight angle AOB is marked on the edge of a paper. The paper is folded so that OB lies exactly on OA, making a crease OC. Which reason best shows that angle AOC and angle COB are right angles?
options: The crease is straight, so any angle beside it is a right angle.
The crease is always at right angles to the longer side of paper.
The two angles overlap exactly, so each is half a straight angle.
Angle AOC looks like the letter L, so it must be a right angle.
explanation: Correct option: (C). Folding superimposes angle COB on angle AOC exactly, so the two angles are equal, and together they make the straight angle AOB; so each is half of a straight angle, which is a right angle. A straight crease alone does not give right angles, folding does not depend on the longer side, and looking like an L is not a proof.

explanation: Correct option: (B). The two angles between the same pair of rays together make a full turn of 360 degrees, so the reflex angle = 360 - 102 = 258 degrees. 78 degrees is 180 - 102, 282 degrees adds 180 to 102, and 162 degrees has no basis.

stem: Puzzle: I am an acute angle with a whole number of degrees. Doubling, tripling or multiplying my measure by 4 still gives an acute angle, but multiplying it by 5 gives an obtuse angle. What are all the possible measures?
explanation: Correct option: (D). Four times the angle must be less than 90, so the angle is less than 22.5 degrees; five times it must be more than 90, so the angle is more than 18 degrees. The whole numbers are 19, 20, 21 and 22 degrees. 18 gives 5 x 18 = 90 (a right angle, not obtuse), and 23 gives 4 x 23 = 92 (obtuse).
